description: I am Dr. Ali Yousuf Khan, an IT professional with a PhD in Telecommunications Engineering. My areas of interest include Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), and Information Technology (IT).
summary:
Earth Pulse Pakistan is an interactive web dashboard that turns more than 25 years of NASA and NOAA Earth observation data into clear, evidence-based trends for Pakistan. It combines MODIS land surface temperature and vegetation (NDVI), sea surface temperature and rainfall for the whole country, its provinces, districts and the coastal Arabian Sea. Users can explore monthly and seasonal patterns, test trends with Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope statistics, and compare variables side by side on a map and charts.
It answers the "Be an Earth System Trend Detector" challenge by helping anyone separate real long-term change from ordinary year-to-year variability. Every chart states its data source and limits, missing months are shown as gaps rather than filled, and nothing is simulated.
This matters because Pakistan is among the countries most exposed to heatwaves, floods and food-water stress. Farmers, planners, researchers and communities need trustworthy, accessible climate evidence to prepare and adapt. Earth Pulse Pakistan makes NASA's long satellite record understandable and usable, turning open data into early, practical insight for decisions on agriculture, water, health and coastal resilience.
details:
What does your project do, and how does it work?

Earth Pulse Pakistan is a web dashboard that detects long-term environmental trends across Pakistan. It combines land surface temperature (day and night) and vegetation greenness (NDVI) from NASA’s MODIS satellite, sea surface temperature from NOAA, and rainfall. A data pipeline retrieves these records through Microsoft Planetary Computer, averages the valid pixels inside each region for every month since 2000, and saves them as plain data files. The dashboard lets users choose a region, time window and farming season (Kharif or Rabi), view results on a map and 3D globe, and run trend tests (Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope) and variable-to-variable comparisons. Months without data appear as gaps, never as estimates.

What benefits does it have?

Earth Pulse Pakistan puts scattered satellite records in one place and answers a simple question: is this a real trend or normal variation? Users get plain-language results with the statistics behind them, so non-experts can understand the evidence and experts can check it. Every chart names its source, product and limitations. It uses only open data, needs no accounts, and organises results around seasons that matter to Pakistani agriculture. Teams no longer have to download, clean and process large satellite archives themselves.
